questions.question: A CPU-bound AWS Lambda function takes 1.5 seconds to run with 512 MB of memory. The team wants to reduce the duration with the smallest configuration change. Which change should a solutions architect make?
options: Set a reserved concurrency value so that the function receives dedicated CPU
Increase the function's memory setting, which also increases the CPU power allocated to it
Enable provisioned concurrency so that the function code runs faster on each request
Increase the function's timeout so that the function has more time to finish
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because Lambda allocates CPU power in proportion to the configured memory, so more memory usually shortens the duration of CPU-bound code. Option A is incorrect because reserved concurrency controls how many executions can run and does not allocate CPU. Option C is incorrect because provisioned concurrency removes initialization delays but does not speed up the code itself. Option D is incorrect because the timeout is only a limit and does not change the speed of execution. Takeaway: tune Lambda memory to tune CPU.

questions.question: Developers are allowed to launch Amazon EC2 instances with instance profiles. The security team wants developers to be able to attach only roles whose names begin with app- and to be unable to launch instances with a highly privileged administrator role. Which IAM permission design meets this requirement?
options: Grant ec2:RunInstances and grant sts:AssumeRole on roles that match app-* so that developers can attach them to instances
Grant ec2:RunInstances and grant iam:GetRole and iam:ListInstanceProfiles on roles that match app-*
Grant ec2:RunInstances and grant iam:PassRole with the Resource set to arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/app-*
Grant ec2:RunInstances and grant iam:PassRole with the Resource set to * and rely on developers to choose the right role
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because launching a resource with a role requires the iam:PassRole permission on that role, and restricting its Resource element limits which roles the developer can pass. Option A is incorrect because sts:AssumeRole lets a principal assume a role itself; it does not authorize passing a role to a service. Option B is incorrect because read permissions such as GetRole do not grant the ability to attach a role. Option D is incorrect because a wildcard resource lets developers pass any role, including administrator roles. Takeaway: scope iam:PassRole to specific role ARNs to prevent privilege escalation.

questions.question: An Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database runs complex reporting queries that create large temporary tables and sort operations. The queries are slow because temporary data spills to network-attached storage. The team wants faster query processing without changing the queries. Which change helps the MOST?
options: Enable Multi-AZ so that the temporary tables are stored on the standby instance
Use a DB instance class with local NVMe SSD storage and enable RDS Optimized Reads
Add a read replica in another Region and run the reporting queries against the replica
Increase the provisioned IOPS of the database storage volume to the highest available value
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because Optimized Reads places temporary tables and caches on local NVMe SSD storage of supported instance classes, which speeds up queries that spill to disk. Option A is incorrect because the standby instance does not process queries. Option C is incorrect because a cross-Region replica adds latency and does not speed up the temporary table operations of the queries. Option D is incorrect because more IOPS on network storage does not remove the latency of remote temporary storage. Takeaway: use local NVMe with Optimized Reads for temporary-data-heavy queries.

questions.question: A nightly Amazon ECS batch workload runs stateless tasks on AWS Fargate. The tasks can be retried if they fail and tolerate interruption with a two-minute warning. The company wants to lower the compute cost of these tasks. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Purchase Fargate Reserved Capacity for the batch tasks so that the tasks run at a discounted rate
Run the tasks on Fargate with the smallest task size and no capacity provider, so that each task costs less
Run the tasks with a Fargate Spot capacity provider so that they use spare capacity at a discount
Run the tasks on On-Demand Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group that scales to zero when idle
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because Fargate Spot runs tasks on spare capacity at a significant discount and sends a two-minute termination notice, which fits retryable, interruption-tolerant tasks. Option A is incorrect because there is no Fargate Reserved Capacity offering. Option B is incorrect because a smaller size lowers the cost per task only if the task can run with fewer resources, and it does not use discounted capacity. Option D is incorrect because On-Demand EC2 adds instance management and is not cheaper for this pattern. Takeaway: use Fargate Spot for fault-tolerant container workloads.

questions.question: A gaming company stores player profiles in Amazon DynamoDB in us-east-1. Players in Europe and Asia must be able to read and write their profiles with low latency from their nearest Region, and the data must remain available if a Region fails. The company wants the LEAST operational effort. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create on-demand backups of the table, and restore them to the other Regions every hour on a schedule
Convert the table to a global table with replicas in the other Regions, and have each Region use its local replica
Deploy a DAX cluster in each Region in front of the table that is located in us-east-1 for local reads
Create separate tables in each Region, and use DynamoDB Streams with Lambda functions to copy changes between them
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because global tables provide fully managed multi-Region, multi-active replication, so each Region can serve local reads and writes and survive a Regional failure. Option A is incorrect because periodic restores produce stale, read-only copies and an hourly recovery point. Option C is incorrect because DAX is a read cache in one Region and does not provide local writes or Regional resilience. Option D is incorrect because custom replication with Streams and Lambda requires building conflict handling and operations that global tables provide. Takeaway: use global tables for multi-Region active-active DynamoDB workloads.

questions.question: A product catalog stored in Amazon DynamoDB receives millions of eventually consistent reads for a small set of popular items. The team wants response times in microseconds and wants to keep the DynamoDB API and change only the client endpoint. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Increase the table's provisioned read capacity units so that reads are served from faster storage
Deploy an Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster and point the DynamoDB client to the DAX endpoint
Deploy Amazon ElastiCache for Redis and rewrite the application to check the cache before reading the table
Convert the table to a global table so that reads are served from the nearest replica
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because DAX is an in-memory, API-compatible cache for DynamoDB that returns cached items in microseconds, and only the endpoint needs to change. Option A is incorrect because more read capacity avoids throttling but does not lower single-digit millisecond latency to microseconds. Option C is incorrect because ElastiCache works but requires application changes to implement the caching logic. Option D is incorrect because global tables reduce distance for global users and do not provide an in-memory cache. Takeaway: DAX accelerates read-heavy DynamoDB workloads without code changes to the data model.

questions.question: Workers process messages from an Amazon SQS standard queue. Processing takes up to 90 seconds, but the queue uses the default visibility timeout of 30 seconds. Some messages are processed twice by different workers. What should a solutions architect change?
options: Increase the queue's visibility timeout to more than the maximum processing time
Reduce the message retention period so that old messages are removed sooner
Configure a delay queue of 90 seconds so that workers receive messages later
Enable long polling so that workers receive each message only once
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because a message that is not deleted before its visibility timeout expires becomes visible again and another worker can receive it; a timeout longer than the processing time prevents that. Option B is incorrect because retention determines how long unprocessed messages stay in the queue. Option C is incorrect because a delay queue postpones the first delivery of every message and does not protect messages that are being processed. Option D is incorrect because long polling reduces empty receives and does not affect redelivery of in-flight messages. Takeaway: set the visibility timeout above the worst-case processing time, or extend it while processing.
